Ils excellent également dans la préparation des peaux, la confection de vêtements de cuir, la fabrication de cordes et l’usage des plantes. Le métal est plus rare et souvent obtenu par échange. Compléments 39

Les Hommes des Bois privilégient les armes adaptées à la chasse et aux embuscades : arc, lance, javelot, hachette, couteau, bâton et gourdin.

Compléments 40

Ils portent rarement des armures lourdes, qui gênent les déplacements dans les arbres et les sous-bois. Le cuir, les vêtements renforcés et quelques pièces de maille sont plus courants.

Compléments 41

Ils évitent les batailles rangées lorsque la forêt leur permet de harceler l’ennemi, de couper ses lignes et de l’attirer dans une embuscade.

Compléments 42

Les enfants apprennent très tôt à reconnaître les traces, identifier les plantes, grimper, se cacher, fabriquer un feu discret, trouver de l’eau, utiliser un arc, éviter les prédateurs et se repérer sous les arbres.

Les Hommes des Bois incarnent une culture de survie, de silence et de vigilance. Leur force ne réside ni dans les villes ni dans les armées nombreuses, mais dans leur capacité à faire corps avec la forêt. Là où un étranger ne voit qu’un mur d’arbres et d’ombres, eux distinguent des routes, des refuges, des signes et des frontières invisibles.

  • Westron — Parlée 6 / Écrite 4
  • Sindarin — Parlée 4 / Écrite 3

Woodmen

The Woodmen are descendants of ancient Eriadorians who crossed the Misty Mountains during the Second Age, pushed eastward by the expansion of Númenórean colonies. They found refuge in the vast forests of Rhovanion and gradually settled beneath the canopy of the great forest later called Mirkwood. Over generations they almost entirely abandoned the customs of open country and became a forest people, shaped by the shadow of trees, hidden clearings, and invisible paths.

Origins

They belong to the Northmen and are related to the Berninga of the Anduin valleys as well as to peoples established near the foothills of the Grey Mountains. Geographic and cultural proximity encourages alliances, trade, and occasional marriages, even though the Woodmen remain more secretive, more settled, and more closely tied to the deep forest.

Appearance

Woodmen are generally tall and solidly built. Their builds range from average to stocky, with strong, angular features. Men often reach nearly six feet one inch and frequently wear full beards. Women are shorter but remain robust and accustomed to physical work.

Communities

Their skin is fair, often marked by ruddy or coppery tones from cold, wind, and outdoor life. Their hair is most often blond, sometimes tending toward red, while their eyes are blue or green. Their life expectancy is comparable to that of other Northmen, generally between sixty-five and eighty-five years.

Resources of the forest

Woodmen live in small, tightly knit groups: extended families, bands, clans, or communities gathered around a few households. Their settlements are concealed in protected clearings, at the foot of great trees, on platforms built in the branches, or in semi-buried dwellings covered with earth and vegetation.

Mastery of trees

Their villages are rarely visible from a path. Entrances are deliberately hard to spot, trails are erased or diverted, and inhabitants use vegetation as their first line of defense. A community may seem nonexistent from only a few dozen paces away, so well do its houses, palisades, and shelters blend into the undergrowth.

Organization

Construction favors local timber, branches, bark, earth, rough stone, hides, and furs. Buildings are simple but sturdy, designed to withstand rain, cold, and sudden attacks. Stores are often distributed among several caches so that a raid or fire cannot deprive the whole clan of food.

Family

Woodmen draw most of their resources from the forest. They hunt, fish, gather berries, harvest honey, collect mushrooms, and make use of medicinal plants. They also practice a little animal husbandry and cultivate small plots in the best-protected clearings.

Temperament

Their diet is based in particular on game, fish, roots, wild fruit, honey, grain grown in small quantities, and products from livestock.

Relations

They know the seasons of animal migration, fruiting periods, dangerous plants, and signs announcing disease or storm. This knowledge is not reserved for hunters: it forms part of every child's education.

Enemies

No other human people of Rhovanion moves as naturally beneath the trees. Woodmen climb with remarkable ease and know how to pass from branch to branch high above the ground. They move quickly through undergrowth, avoid roots, cross fallen trunks, and use height to observe or fight.

Spirituality

They excel especially at climbing, acrobatics in trees, foraging, tracking, hunting, hiding, stealthy movement, and forest survival.

Magic

Their training among the trees allows them to watch a territory unseen, set an ambush from branches, or escape a creature unable to climb. Their knowledge of edible and medicinal plants is also greater than that of most other human peoples.

Languages

Woodmen possess no centralized political structure. Each band or clan settles its own affairs, chooses its leaders, and defends its territory. Authority generally belongs to elders, renowned hunters, experienced warriors, or members of respected families.

Clothing

A leader does not rule by absolute right. He must persuade, protect, and maintain the unity of the group. Important decisions are discussed within the extended family or before the adults of the clan.

Craftsmanship

This independence makes it difficult to unite several communities even in the face of a common threat. Alliances are often temporary and rest on personal trust, marriages, or oaths. When a major danger appears, however, several clans may gather under the authority of a particularly respected leader.

War

Marriage is monogamous. Descent generally follows the male line, and a wife joins her husband's family. Unions are contracted outside the immediate family but most often within the clan or between allied communities.

Education

The extended family forms the heart of social life. Children are raised collectively, learn the rules of the forest at an early age, and accompany adults on simple tasks. Everyone must know how to be useful, recognize dangers, and contribute to the group's survival.

Place in character creation

Woodmen are quiet, independent, and reserved. They speak little with strangers and avoid revealing the location of their homes. Their distrust comes from centuries of raids, intrusions, and fighting against creatures of the Shadow.

Additional notes 19

They prefer to observe before acting. A traveler can cross their territory without ever seeing them while being watched from the trees for several hours. Those who respect the forest, do not threaten its inhabitants, and behave frankly can earn their trust. Those who cut trees needlessly, hunt without permission, or approach their refuges armed are quickly regarded as enemies.

Additional notes 20

Their reserve should not be confused with coldness. Within the clan they are warm, loyal, and attached to stories, songs, and family festivals.

Additional notes 21

Woodmen chiefly maintain relations with the Berninga and Silvan Elves. The former share their hostility toward creatures of the Shadow and their knowledge of the Anduin valleys. The latter understand their attachment to trees and respect for ancient places.

Additional notes 22

Relations with Elves nevertheless remain tinged with caution. Woodmen admire their wisdom, mastery of the forest, and longevity, but know that the interests of the Firstborn do not always coincide with those of Men.

Additional notes 23

Townsfolk and merchants are received with reserve. Woodmen have little need for coin and readily use barter. A healer may exchange salves for a woolen cloak, a hunter hides for a blade or metal tools.

Additional notes 24

They particularly hate Orcs, Wargs, Trolls, and Giant Spiders. These creatures directly threaten their families, territories, and routes. Giant Spiders inspire particular horror because they corrupt the depths of the forest, block paths, and sometimes carry off isolated travelers or hunters.

Additional notes 25

Woodmen do not always wait for an enemy to approach their village. They organize patrols, destroy lairs, watch suspicious clearings, and place sentries in the trees.

Additional notes 26

Their spirituality is intimate and family-centered. It is expressed in daily gestures, respect for places, songs, and traditions specific to each clan. Great ceremonies bringing together several communities are rare.

Additional notes 27

The central figure in their religious life is often a woman called a Wita, “She Who Knows.” Wuitan serve as healers, seers, counselors, and spiritual guides. They know plants, ritual songs, omens, and the ancient stories of the people.

Additional notes 28

They watch over the Cult of Growth, called Alanakyn, associated with fertility, renewal, trees, and natural cycles. Its great ceremonies are rare and may gather several clans in a sacred clearing.

Additional notes 29

Among the Valar, the Woodmen chiefly honor Araw, their name for Oromë. They see him as hunter, rider, and protector of those who travel the wild lands.

Additional notes 30

Magic is rare and closely tied to the tradition of the Wuitan. Their powers do not take the form of scholarly incantations or written formulae: they are sung, chanted, or whispered.

Additional notes 31

Songs may accompany healing, divination, protection of a home, plant growth, calming an animal, finding a path, and seasonal ceremonies.

Additional notes 32

Women may follow the path of the Wuitan, close to Animists but with practices blending healing, visions, and Ranger traditions. Other members of the community may pursue almost every profession, but magical practices remain unusual and strongly dependent on acceptance by the clan.

Additional notes 33

Nahaiduk, a language of Rhovanion, is their principal tongue. Most also know some Westron and Sindarin.

Additional notes 34

Depending on region and contacts, they may learn the Atliduk of the Berninga, Logathig, Westron, and Sindarin. Those living near Elven communities naturally know more Sindarin, while those trading with the Anduin valleys have a stronger command of Atliduk.

Additional notes 35

Their clothing is simple, sturdy, and suited to the forest. They wear coarse woolen tunics, short trousers with leggings, and coats, cloaks, and caps of fur.

Additional notes 36

Preferred colors are those that blend into the surroundings: brown, grey, dark green, beige, russet, and black. Hooded cloaks are common. Hunters use quiet clothing and avoid ornaments that might catch on branches or reflect light.

Additional notes 37

Woodworking naturally holds a central place. Woodmen make bows, arrows, spears, traps, tools, containers, furniture, shelters, light boats, and ritual objects.

Additional notes 38

They also excel at preparing hides, making leather clothing, ropework, and use of plants. Metal is rarer and often obtained through trade. A good blade, axe, or spearhead is a valuable possession handed down within a family.

Additional notes 39

Woodmen favor weapons suited to hunting and ambush: bow, spear, javelin, hatchet, knife, staff, and club.

Additional notes 40

They rarely wear heavy armor, which hinders movement in trees and undergrowth. Leather, reinforced clothing, and a few pieces of mail are more common.

Additional notes 41

Their way of fighting relies on surprise, concealment, shooting from trees, rapid attacks, use of terrain, and withdrawal along known paths. They avoid pitched battles when the forest lets them harass the enemy, cut its lines, and draw it into ambush.

Additional notes 42

Children learn very early to recognize tracks, identify plants, climb, hide, make a discreet fire, find water, use a bow, avoid predators, and find their way beneath the trees.

Additional notes 43

This Culture is particularly suitable for a character from a hunting clan of Mirkwood, a fortified clearing, a family living in the trees, a community near the Berninga, a group in contact with Silvan Elves, a line of Wuitan, or a band charged with watching Giant Spiders.

Additional notes 44

The Woodmen embody a culture of survival, silence, and vigilance. Their strength lies neither in cities nor in numerous armies, but in their ability to become one with the forest. Where an outsider sees only a wall of trees and shadows, they distinguish roads, refuges, signs, and invisible boundaries.

  • Nahaiduk — Spoken 8 / Written 6
  • Westron — Spoken 6 / Written 4
  • Sindarin — Spoken 4 / Written 3

Hommes des Bois

Les Hommes des Bois sont les descendants d’anciens Eriadoriens qui franchirent les Monts Brumeux durant le Deuxième Âge, repoussés vers l’est par l’expansion des colonies númenóréennes. Ils trouvèrent refuge dans les vastes forêts du Rhovanion et s’établirent peu à peu sous les frondaisons de la grande forêt appelée plus tard Forêt Noire. Au fil des générations, ils abandonnèrent presque entièrement les usages des terres ouvertes pour devenir un peuple forestier, façonné par l’ombre des arbres, les clairières cachées et les sentiers invisibles.

Origines

Ils appartiennent aux Hommes du Nord et sont apparentés aux Béornides des vallées de l’Anduin ainsi qu’aux peuples établis près des contreforts des Montagnes Grises. Leur proximité géographique et culturelle favorise les alliances, les échanges et les mariages occasionnels, même si les Hommes des Bois restent plus secrets, plus sédentaires et davantage liés à la forêt profonde.

Apparence

Les Hommes des Bois sont généralement grands et solidement bâtis. Leur silhouette va de moyenne à trapue, avec des traits anguleux et vigoureux. Les hommes atteignent souvent près d’un mètre quatre-vingt-cinq et portent fréquemment une barbe abondante. Les femmes sont plus petites, mais restent robustes et habituées aux travaux physiques.

Communautés

Leur peau est claire, souvent marquée de reflets roux ou cuivrés par le froid, le vent et la vie au grand air. Leurs cheveux sont le plus souvent blonds, parfois tirant vers le roux, tandis que leurs yeux sont bleus ou verts. Leur espérance de vie est comparable à celle des autres Hommes du Nord, généralement comprise entre soixante-cinq et quatre-vingt-cinq ans.

Ressources de la forêt

Les Hommes des Bois vivent en petits groupes étroitement unis : familles élargies, bandes, clans ou communautés réunies autour de quelques maisonnées. Leurs établissements sont dissimulés dans des clairières protégées, au pied de grands arbres, sur des plateformes construites dans les branches ou dans des habitations semi-enterrées recouvertes de terre et de végétation.

Maîtrise des arbres

Leurs villages sont rarement visibles depuis un chemin. Les accès sont volontairement difficiles à repérer, les sentiers sont effacés ou détournés, et les habitants utilisent la végétation comme première ligne de défense. Une communauté peut sembler inexistante à quelques dizaines de pas seulement, tant ses maisons, ses palissades et ses abris se confondent avec le sous-bois.

Organisation

Les constructions privilégient le bois local, les branchages, l’écorce, la terre, la pierre brute, les peaux et les fourrures. Les bâtiments sont simples mais solides, conçus pour résister aux pluies, au froid et aux attaques soudaines. Les réserves sont souvent réparties dans plusieurs caches afin qu’un raid ou un incendie ne prive pas tout le clan de nourriture.

Famille

Les Hommes des Bois tirent l’essentiel de leurs ressources de la forêt. Ils chassent, pêchent, cueillent les baies, récoltent le miel, ramassent les champignons et exploitent les plantes médicinales. Ils pratiquent aussi un peu d’élevage et cultivent de petites parcelles dans les clairières les mieux protégées.

Tempérament

Leur alimentation repose notamment sur le gibier, le poisson, les racines, les fruits sauvages, le miel, les céréales cultivées en faible quantité et les produits issus de l’élevage.

Relations

Ils connaissent les saisons de migration des animaux, les périodes de fructification, les plantes dangereuses et les signes annonçant une maladie ou une tempête. Cette connaissance n’est pas réservée aux chasseurs : elle fait partie de l’éducation de chaque enfant.

Ennemis

Nul autre peuple humain du Rhovanion ne se déplace aussi naturellement sous les arbres. Les Hommes des Bois grimpent avec une aisance remarquable et savent progresser d’une branche à l’autre bien au-dessus du sol. Ils se déplacent vite dans les sous-bois, évitent les racines, franchissent les troncs tombés et utilisent les hauteurs pour observer ou combattre.

Spiritualité

Ils excellent particulièrement dans l’escalade, l’acrobatie dans les arbres, la cueillette, le pistage, la chasse, la dissimulation, le déplacement furtif et la survie forestière.

Magie

Leur formation dans les arbres leur permet de surveiller un territoire sans se montrer, de tendre une embuscade depuis les branches ou d’échapper à une créature incapable de grimper. Leur connaissance des plantes comestibles et médicinales est également supérieure à celle de la plupart des autres peuples humains.

Langues

Les Hommes des Bois ne possèdent pas de structure politique centralisée. Chaque bande ou clan règle ses propres affaires, choisit ses chefs et défend son territoire. L’autorité appartient généralement aux anciens, aux chasseurs réputés, aux guerriers expérimentés ou aux membres de familles respectées.

Vêtements

Un chef ne gouverne pas par droit absolu. Il doit convaincre, protéger et maintenir l’unité du groupe. Les décisions importantes sont discutées au sein de la famille élargie ou devant les adultes du clan.

Artisanat

Cette indépendance rend difficile l’unification de plusieurs communautés, même face à une menace commune. Les alliances sont souvent temporaires et reposent sur la confiance personnelle, les mariages ou les serments. Lorsqu’un danger majeur apparaît, cependant, plusieurs clans peuvent se réunir sous l’autorité d’un chef particulièrement respecté.

Guerre

Le mariage est monogame. La filiation suit généralement la lignée masculine, et l’épouse rejoint la famille de son mari. Les unions se concluent à l’extérieur de la famille immédiate, mais le plus souvent à l’intérieur du clan ou entre communautés alliées.

Éducation

Hommes des Bois

Les Hommes des Bois sont les descendants d’anciens Eriadoriens qui franchirent les Monts Brumeux durant le Deuxième Âge, repoussés vers l’est par l’expansion des colonies númenóréennes. Ils trouvèrent refuge dans les vastes forêts du Rhovanion et s’établirent peu à peu sous les frondaisons de la grande forêt appelée plus tard Forêt Noire. Au fil des générations, ils abandonnèrent presque entièrement les usages des terres ouvertes pour devenir un peuple forestier, façonné par l’ombre des arbres, les clairières cachées et les sentiers invisibles.

Origines

Ils appartiennent aux Hommes du Nord et sont apparentés aux Béornides des vallées de l’Anduin ainsi qu’aux peuples établis près des contreforts des Montagnes Grises. Leur proximité géographique et culturelle favorise les alliances, les échanges et les mariages occasionnels, même si les Hommes des Bois restent plus secrets, plus sédentaires et davantage liés à la forêt profonde.

Apparence

Les Hommes des Bois sont généralement grands et solidement bâtis. Leur silhouette va de moyenne à trapue, avec des traits anguleux et vigoureux. Les hommes atteignent souvent près d’un mètre quatre-vingt-cinq et portent fréquemment une barbe abondante. Les femmes sont plus petites, mais restent robustes et habituées aux travaux physiques.

Communautés

Leur peau est claire, souvent marquée de reflets roux ou cuivrés par le froid, le vent et la vie au grand air. Leurs cheveux sont le plus souvent blonds, parfois tirant vers le roux, tandis que leurs yeux sont bleus ou verts. Leur espérance de vie est comparable à celle des autres Hommes du Nord, généralement comprise entre soixante-cinq et quatre-vingt-cinq ans.

Ressources de la forêt

Les Hommes des Bois vivent en petits groupes étroitement unis : familles élargies, bandes, clans ou communautés réunies autour de quelques maisonnées. Leurs établissements sont dissimulés dans des clairières protégées, au pied de grands arbres, sur des plateformes construites dans les branches ou dans des habitations semi-enterrées recouvertes de terre et de végétation.

Maîtrise des arbres

Leurs villages sont rarement visibles depuis un chemin. Les accès sont volontairement difficiles à repérer, les sentiers sont effacés ou détournés, et les habitants utilisent la végétation comme première ligne de défense. Une communauté peut sembler inexistante à quelques dizaines de pas seulement, tant ses maisons, ses palissades et ses abris se confondent avec le sous-bois.

Organisation

Les constructions privilégient le bois local, les branchages, l’écorce, la terre, la pierre brute, les peaux et les fourrures. Les bâtiments sont simples mais solides, conçus pour résister aux pluies, au froid et aux attaques soudaines. Les réserves sont souvent réparties dans plusieurs caches afin qu’un raid ou un incendie ne prive pas tout le clan de nourriture.

Famille

Les Hommes des Bois tirent l’essentiel de leurs ressources de la forêt. Ils chassent, pêchent, cueillent les baies, récoltent le miel, ramassent les champignons et exploitent les plantes médicinales. Ils pratiquent aussi un peu d’élevage et cultivent de petites parcelles dans les clairières les mieux protégées.

Tempérament

Leur alimentation repose notamment sur le gibier, le poisson, les racines, les fruits sauvages, le miel, les céréales cultivées en faible quantité et les produits issus de l’élevage.

Relations

Ils connaissent les saisons de migration des animaux, les périodes de fructification, les plantes dangereuses et les signes annonçant une maladie ou une tempête. Cette connaissance n’est pas réservée aux chasseurs : elle fait partie de l’éducation de chaque enfant.

Ennemis

Nul autre peuple humain du Rhovanion ne se déplace aussi naturellement sous les arbres. Les Hommes des Bois grimpent avec une aisance remarquable et savent progresser d’une branche à l’autre bien au-dessus du sol. Ils se déplacent vite dans les sous-bois, évitent les racines, franchissent les troncs tombés et utilisent les hauteurs pour observer ou combattre.

Spiritualité

Ils excellent particulièrement dans l’escalade, l’acrobatie dans les arbres, la cueillette, le pistage, la chasse, la dissimulation, le déplacement furtif et la survie forestière.

Magie

Leur formation dans les arbres leur permet de surveiller un territoire sans se montrer, de tendre une embuscade depuis les branches ou d’échapper à une créature incapable de grimper. Leur connaissance des plantes comestibles et médicinales est également supérieure à celle de la plupart des autres peuples humains.

Langues

Les Hommes des Bois ne possèdent pas de structure politique centralisée. Chaque bande ou clan règle ses propres affaires, choisit ses chefs et défend son territoire. L’autorité appartient généralement aux anciens, aux chasseurs réputés, aux guerriers expérimentés ou aux membres de familles respectées.

Vêtements

Un chef ne gouverne pas par droit absolu. Il doit convaincre, protéger et maintenir l’unité du groupe. Les décisions importantes sont discutées au sein de la famille élargie ou devant les adultes du clan.

Artisanat

Cette indépendance rend difficile l’unification de plusieurs communautés, même face à une menace commune. Les alliances sont souvent temporaires et reposent sur la confiance personnelle, les mariages ou les serments. Lorsqu’un danger majeur apparaît, cependant, plusieurs clans peuvent se réunir sous l’autorité d’un chef particulièrement respecté.

Guerre

Le mariage est monogame. La filiation suit généralement la lignée masculine, et l’épouse rejoint la famille de son mari. Les unions se concluent à l’extérieur de la famille immédiate, mais le plus souvent à l’intérieur du clan ou entre communautés alliées.

Éducation

La famille élargie constitue le cœur de la vie sociale. Les enfants sont élevés collectivement, apprennent très tôt les règles de la forêt et accompagnent les adultes lors de tâches simples. Chacun doit savoir se rendre utile, reconnaître les dangers et contribuer à la survie du groupe.

Les Hommes des Bois sont silencieux, indépendants et réservés. Ils parlent peu avec les étrangers et évitent de dévoiler l’emplacement de leurs demeures. Leur méfiance vient de siècles de raids, d’intrusions et de combats contre les créatures de l’Ombre.

Woodmen

The Woodmen are descendants of ancient Eriadorians who crossed the Misty Mountains during the Second Age, pushed eastward by the expansion of Númenórean colonies. They found refuge in the vast forests of Rhovanion and gradually settled beneath the canopy of the great forest later called Mirkwood. Over generations they almost entirely abandoned the customs of open country and became a forest people, shaped by the shadow of trees, hidden clearings, and invisible paths.

Origins

They belong to the Northmen and are related to the Berninga of the Anduin valleys as well as to peoples established near the foothills of the Grey Mountains. Geographic and cultural proximity encourages alliances, trade, and occasional marriages, even though the Woodmen remain more secretive, more settled, and more closely tied to the deep forest.

Appearance

Woodmen are generally tall and solidly built. Their builds range from average to stocky, with strong, angular features. Men often reach nearly six feet one inch and frequently wear full beards. Women are shorter but remain robust and accustomed to physical work.

Communities

Their skin is fair, often marked by ruddy or coppery tones from cold, wind, and outdoor life. Their hair is most often blond, sometimes tending toward red, while their eyes are blue or green. Their life expectancy is comparable to that of other Northmen, generally between sixty-five and eighty-five years.

Resources of the forest

Woodmen live in small, tightly knit groups: extended families, bands, clans, or communities gathered around a few households. Their settlements are concealed in protected clearings, at the foot of great trees, on platforms built in the branches, or in semi-buried dwellings covered with earth and vegetation.

Mastery of trees

Their villages are rarely visible from a path. Entrances are deliberately hard to spot, trails are erased or diverted, and inhabitants use vegetation as their first line of defense. A community may seem nonexistent from only a few dozen paces away, so well do its houses, palisades, and shelters blend into the undergrowth.

Organization

Construction favors local timber, branches, bark, earth, rough stone, hides, and furs. Buildings are simple but sturdy, designed to withstand rain, cold, and sudden attacks. Stores are often distributed among several caches so that a raid or fire cannot deprive the whole clan of food.

Family

Woodmen draw most of their resources from the forest. They hunt, fish, gather berries, harvest honey, collect mushrooms, and make use of medicinal plants. They also practice a little animal husbandry and cultivate small plots in the best-protected clearings.

Temperament

Their diet is based in particular on game, fish, roots, wild fruit, honey, grain grown in small quantities, and products from livestock.

Relations

They know the seasons of animal migration, fruiting periods, dangerous plants, and signs announcing disease or storm. This knowledge is not reserved for hunters: it forms part of every child's education.

Enemies

No other human people of Rhovanion moves as naturally beneath the trees. Woodmen climb with remarkable ease and know how to pass from branch to branch high above the ground. They move quickly through undergrowth, avoid roots, cross fallen trunks, and use height to observe or fight.

Spirituality

They excel especially at climbing, acrobatics in trees, foraging, tracking, hunting, hiding, stealthy movement, and forest survival.

Magic

Their training among the trees allows them to watch a territory unseen, set an ambush from branches, or escape a creature unable to climb. Their knowledge of edible and medicinal plants is also greater than that of most other human peoples.

Languages

Woodmen possess no centralized political structure. Each band or clan settles its own affairs, chooses its leaders, and defends its territory. Authority generally belongs to elders, renowned hunters, experienced warriors, or members of respected families.

Clothing

A leader does not rule by absolute right. He must persuade, protect, and maintain the unity of the group. Important decisions are discussed within the extended family or before the adults of the clan.

Craftsmanship

This independence makes it difficult to unite several communities even in the face of a common threat. Alliances are often temporary and rest on personal trust, marriages, or oaths. When a major danger appears, however, several clans may gather under the authority of a particularly respected leader.

War

Marriage is monogamous. Descent generally follows the male line, and a wife joins her husband's family. Unions are contracted outside the immediate family but most often within the clan or between allied communities.

Education

The extended family forms the heart of social life. Children are raised collectively, learn the rules of the forest at an early age, and accompany adults on simple tasks. Everyone must know how to be useful, recognize dangers, and contribute to the group's survival.

Place in character creation

Woodmen are quiet, independent, and reserved. They speak little with strangers and avoid revealing the location of their homes. Their distrust comes from centuries of raids, intrusions, and fighting against creatures of the Shadow.

Additional notes 19

They prefer to observe before acting. A traveler can cross their territory without ever seeing them while being watched from the trees for several hours. Those who respect the forest, do not threaten its inhabitants, and behave frankly can earn their trust. Those who cut trees needlessly, hunt without permission, or approach their refuges armed are quickly regarded as enemies.

Additional notes 20

Their reserve should not be confused with coldness. Within the clan they are warm, loyal, and attached to stories, songs, and family festivals.

Additional notes 21

Woodmen chiefly maintain relations with the Berninga and Silvan Elves. The former share their hostility toward creatures of the Shadow and their knowledge of the Anduin valleys. The latter understand their attachment to trees and respect for ancient places.

Additional notes 22

Relations with Elves nevertheless remain tinged with caution. Woodmen admire their wisdom, mastery of the forest, and longevity, but know that the interests of the Firstborn do not always coincide with those of Men.

Additional notes 23

Townsfolk and merchants are received with reserve. Woodmen have little need for coin and readily use barter. A healer may exchange salves for a woolen cloak, a hunter hides for a blade or metal tools.

Additional notes 24

They particularly hate Orcs, Wargs, Trolls, and Giant Spiders. These creatures directly threaten their families, territories, and routes. Giant Spiders inspire particular horror because they corrupt the depths of the forest, block paths, and sometimes carry off isolated travelers or hunters.

Additional notes 25

Woodmen do not always wait for an enemy to approach their village. They organize patrols, destroy lairs, watch suspicious clearings, and place sentries in the trees.

Additional notes 26

Their spirituality is intimate and family-centered. It is expressed in daily gestures, respect for places, songs, and traditions specific to each clan. Great ceremonies bringing together several communities are rare.

Additional notes 27

The central figure in their religious life is often a woman called a Wita, “She Who Knows.” Wuitan serve as healers, seers, counselors, and spiritual guides. They know plants, ritual songs, omens, and the ancient stories of the people.

Additional notes 28

They watch over the Cult of Growth, called Alanakyn, associated with fertility, renewal, trees, and natural cycles. Its great ceremonies are rare and may gather several clans in a sacred clearing.

Additional notes 29

Among the Valar, the Woodmen chiefly honor Araw, their name for Oromë. They see him as hunter, rider, and protector of those who travel the wild lands.

Additional notes 30

Magic is rare and closely tied to the tradition of the Wuitan. Their powers do not take the form of scholarly incantations or written formulae: they are sung, chanted, or whispered.

Additional notes 31

Songs may accompany healing, divination, protection of a home, plant growth, calming an animal, finding a path, and seasonal ceremonies.

Additional notes 32

Women may follow the path of the Wuitan, close to Animists but with practices blending healing, visions, and Ranger traditions. Other members of the community may pursue almost every profession, but magical practices remain unusual and strongly dependent on acceptance by the clan.

Additional notes 33

Nahaiduk, a language of Rhovanion, is their principal tongue. Most also know some Westron and Sindarin.

Additional notes 34

Depending on region and contacts, they may learn the Atliduk of the Berninga, Logathig, Westron, and Sindarin. Those living near Elven communities naturally know more Sindarin, while those trading with the Anduin valleys have a stronger command of Atliduk.

Additional notes 35

Their clothing is simple, sturdy, and suited to the forest. They wear coarse woolen tunics, short trousers with leggings, and coats, cloaks, and caps of fur.

Additional notes 36

Preferred colors are those that blend into the surroundings: brown, grey, dark green, beige, russet, and black. Hooded cloaks are common. Hunters use quiet clothing and avoid ornaments that might catch on branches or reflect light.

Additional notes 37

Woodworking naturally holds a central place. Woodmen make bows, arrows, spears, traps, tools, containers, furniture, shelters, light boats, and ritual objects.

Additional notes 38

They also excel at preparing hides, making leather clothing, ropework, and use of plants. Metal is rarer and often obtained through trade. A good blade, axe, or spearhead is a valuable possession handed down within a family.

Additional notes 39

Woodmen favor weapons suited to hunting and ambush: bow, spear, javelin, hatchet, knife, staff, and club.

Additional notes 40

They rarely wear heavy armor, which hinders movement in trees and undergrowth. Leather, reinforced clothing, and a few pieces of mail are more common.

Additional notes 41

Their way of fighting relies on surprise, concealment, shooting from trees, rapid attacks, use of terrain, and withdrawal along known paths. They avoid pitched battles when the forest lets them harass the enemy, cut its lines, and draw it into ambush.

Additional notes 42

Children learn very early to recognize tracks, identify plants, climb, hide, make a discreet fire, find water, use a bow, avoid predators, and find their way beneath the trees.

Additional notes 43

This Culture is particularly suitable for a character from a hunting clan of Mirkwood, a fortified clearing, a family living in the trees, a community near the Berninga, a group in contact with Silvan Elves, a line of Wuitan, or a band charged with watching Giant Spiders.

Additional notes 44

The Woodmen embody a culture of survival, silence, and vigilance. Their strength lies neither in cities nor in numerous armies, but in their ability to become one with the forest. Where an outsider sees only a wall of trees and shadows, they distinguish roads, refuges, signs, and invisible boundaries.
